result:
The rain had been falling for three days, not hard enough to flood anything, just enough to turn the world soft and gray and make every surface sound like it was thinking. I stood under the awning of a closed bakery and watched a pigeon negotiate with a puddle. The bird kept dipping its beak, then shaking its head as if the water had offered an opinion it didn’t care for.

Across the street a man in a yellow raincoat was trying to fold a map that had already decided against being folded. Every time he got one crease right, another corner rebelled. He laughed once, short and surprised, the way people laugh when they realize the object is winning and they don’t actually mind. A woman with a clear umbrella slowed down to watch him. Neither of them spoke. The map kept expanding.

I thought about how much of a life is spent in these small, unfinished negotiations—with weather, with paper, with the particular stubbornness of birds. Most of them never resolve into stories worth telling later. They just happen, and then the light changes, and you walk on with damp cuffs and the faint sense that something almost clarified itself and then chose not to.

The pigeon finally drank. The man gave up and stuffed the map into his pocket, where it would stay wrinkled and half-useful. The woman kept walking. I stepped out from under the awning. The rain was warmer than it looked.
